Joy, a little white dog, is helping an angler by the river, and a heron keeps stealing the worms he uses as bait. Joy and the heron get into a real tug of war over the food. Later Joy finds out why the heron is so hungry: it is feeding up its crane chicks. Instead of fighting, Joy shares, and in the end the kindness comes back to Joy. The message is simple: what goes around, comes around. If we try to understand why someone behaves badly, we may find a reason, and kindness is usually returned.

The cartoon shows a man on his hands and knees, like a horse. A smiling smartphone is sitting on his back, holding a whip and a rope that goes through the man's nose. The phone is the master and the man is the animal. The artist is saying that many of us are addicted to our phones: we think we control technology, but it controls us. We check it when it 'pulls the rope' with a notification. I agree, because I often pick up my phone without a reason. To break the habit, we should limit our screen time.

A young boy who has been forced to become a child soldier meets a young Masai warrior, and then a lion. With his gun he feels strong, but the lion shows him what real danger is. The Masai boy, who is going through a rite of passage, shows him that true courage is not about holding a weapon or hurting people. It is about facing your fears and protecting others. In the end the boy lays down his weapon. The film says that coming of age means becoming responsible and brave in the right way, not violent.

Two men are resting in the cool shade of a big tree in the middle of a desert. Their axes are next to them, and we can see that they have already cut through the trunk, so the tree is about to fall. When it falls, they will lose their only shade. The artist is criticising short-sighted people who destroy the thing that keeps them alive. This is exactly what deforestation does: we cut down forests for quick money and forget the consequences, like heat, floods and dry land. It is like sawing off the branch you are sitting on.

A student is sitting in an afternoon class and is very drowsy. His eyelids are heavy and his head keeps falling as he dozes off. He fights off sleep in funny ways: his head becomes heavy like a stone, rolls away and bounces back. Every time he almost nods off, he tries hard to keep his eyes open. Everyone who has been to school knows this feeling. The film is a funny, honest picture of how hard it is to concentrate after lunch, and maybe it also says that long, boring lessons make students daydream.

On a seesaw, a girl sits on one side and a boy on the other side holds his heart and a pile of hearts. The hearts are heavy, but the girl doesn't move. In the second picture a rich-looking man in sunglasses puts one dollar sign on the seesaw, and the girl flies towards him. The artist is saying that for some people money outweighs true love. A materialistic person chooses the one who has money, not the one who really loves them. In my opinion this is superficial, and it doesn't last, because money can't buy happiness.

A small sunflower seed falls in a hard, grey place where it seems impossible to grow. Against all odds, it takes root. It faces bad weather and almost withers, but it bounces back each time and finally blooms. At the end it passes on its seeds, so new flowers can grow. The sunflower is a symbol of resilience: life is not always easy, but if we keep going we can grow even in difficult places, and our success can help others after us.

Two men are standing on a train, holding on to the handles. One is a punk with a tall mohawk, earrings and a studded jacket; the other is a bald businessman in a suit and tie. We expect the punk to be the aggressive one, but he is calm and relaxed with his eyes closed, and the businessman looks nervous and afraid of him. The message is: don't judge a book by its cover. First impressions and stereotypes can be wrong, because appearances can be deceiving. Prejudice makes us afraid of people who are different but completely harmless.

On a freezing cold night, someone homeless is trying to keep warm. The little matches in a matchbook decide to help. One by one, they light themselves to give a little heat and a flicker of hope, knowing that a match that burns is gone. They are selfless: they sacrifice themselves to keep someone else warm. The film made me think about people who give everything for others, like parents or volunteers, and how small acts of kindness can make a big difference in someone's darkest moment.

A poor mother is sitting on the floor of an empty room. Her two children are crying because they are hungry. She has nothing to give them, so she cuts a piece of her own body and offers it to them with a fork. The picture is shocking on purpose. The artist shows the self-sacrifice of mothers who live in poverty: they go hungry and give their last strength so their children can eat. It is a picture of unconditional love and of putting others first, and it also reminds us how many families still live like this.

Two rivals want the same thing and each one tries to outsmart the other. They set traps, chase each other and even try to bribe their way to the prize. Every plan backfires, and the fight gets bigger and sillier. Because of their greed, they are so busy fighting each other that they forget what they wanted in the first place, and in the end both of them end up empty-handed. The film shows that when people are greedy and only want to win, everybody loses.

A businessman is running as fast as he can. A stick is tied to his back, and a pile of money is hanging in front of his face, so he can never reach it. He doesn't see that he is running straight towards an open grave. The artist is criticising the rat race: people spend their whole life chasing money and forget to live. Life is short, and in the end we can't take money with us. By working all the time, we dig our own grave. We need a healthy work-life balance.

A group of meerkats live in the desert and look after their beloved fruit, the only one on their little tree. A vulture comes and snatches it. The meerkats don't give up: with great teamwork they chase after the vulture and fight to get their fruit back. But their plan to guard it at any cost backfires in an unexpected way. The film is funny and fast, and it shows two things: together we can do things we can't do alone, and be careful what you wish for, because getting something can bring new problems.

Three prisoners are sitting on a bench. Their heads are padlocks. Two of them look angry and bored, and their locks are closed. The third one is reading a book, and his lock is open. The message is that knowledge is freedom. Education and reading open your mind, even if you are locked up. A narrow-minded person is a prisoner of their own head, but a person who learns can break free. I think this is true outside prison too: books let us see the world and give us choices.

A parent is trying to teach a picky eater to eat healthy food and to behave well. The parent gives lots of rules, but the child sees the parent sneaking and doing exactly what they told the child not to do. Of course, the child copies what the parent does, not what they say. The film is about hypocrisy and about being a role model. If we want children to behave well, we have to lead by example and practise what we preach. Children learn more from our actions than from our words.

Two workers are fixing windows in a building. Outside, the real view is dirty: a factory with chimneys and black smoke. But the workers are putting in new windows with a beautiful picture of a green forest painted on them. Now people inside will see a lovely view and forget the pollution. The artist is criticising people and governments that cover up problems instead of solving them, like sweeping something under the carpet. Out of sight, out of mind: if we can't see the pollution, we pretend it isn't there.

In this world, wishes are granted by little creatures who live under fountains. When someone tosses a coin, the wish granter has to make the wish come true. One wish granter doesn't care about his job, until a young man makes a wish for love. Now he has to go above ground and play matchmaker between two people. He goes out of his way, fails many times, and finally brings them together. The film shows that love sometimes needs a little help, and that doing your job with care can change people's lives.

A book stands on the left and a red brain is walking towards it. But a box with the Instagram logo grabs the brain and pulls it away, while the book can only watch with an exclamation mark. The artist is saying that social media is a strong distraction: it steals our attention from deep reading. Social media addiction makes our attention span shorter, so we scroll for hours but can't read a book for 20 minutes. I recognise this in myself, and I think we need rules for our phone time.

In a grey city, a father, Copi, and his son, Paste, have the same daily routine. The father goes to a boring office job, and the son goes to school, where everyone is the same. The boy loves playing the violin, but school tries to make him fit in, and slowly he loses his spark and his colour, just like his father. When the father sees this, he understands what conformity is doing to his son. He brings him back to the violin player in the park. The film says: don't stifle creativity; follow your passion, not the rat race.

A man and a woman are sitting at opposite ends of a sofa after an argument. Their brains are pulling them back with ropes, but their hearts are walking towards each other. Their minds say 'Don't give up, you are right', but their hearts want to make up. This is the fight of mind versus heart. Because of pride, nobody wants to make the first move, and they both stay stubborn. The cartoon shows that if we listen to our hearts and forget our pride, it is easier to make up with someone we love.

The film is set in a world of chess. A White Knight has to protect his King from the other side, and the enemy is the Red Queen, the woman he loved long ago. They are on opposing sides, so their love is forbidden, and they have to fight. But when the moment comes, he breaks the rules and follows his heart instead of his duty. The film is about the conflict between love and loyalty, and it asks whether rules are more important than our feelings.

A man is sitting in an armchair, and a TV has long arms coming out of its screen. The arms are pouring a bin full of rubbish into the man's head, which is open like a can. The man sits still and doesn't stop it. The artist is saying that TV, and today the internet too, fills our heads with junk. Mindless entertainment is a kind of brainwashing if we just watch and never think. The solution is critical thinking: choose carefully what you watch and question what you hear.

Two girls are best friends. After something bad happens, one of them is overwhelmed by her emotions, and they become a dark magic cloud around her that pushes everyone away. She shuts her friend out, and they start to drift apart. But her friend doesn't give up. She reaches out again and again, even when it hurts, until she breaks the spell. The film shows that when people we love are struggling, they need emotional support. Being there for someone, even when they push you away, can save them.

It is snowing and freezing cold. A poor father is kneeling in the snow. He has taken off his coat and is using it and his own body to shelter his two small children, who are safe and warm underneath. His back is naked in the snow, but he is smiling. The cartoon shows a father's love: he is ready to suffer the cold so his children are protected. It reminds me of all the parents who make a sacrifice every day that their children never see.

Mr Indifferent sees people around him who need help, but he is indifferent: he turns a blind eye and walks past, like a bystander. Every time he ignores someone, his world becomes greyer and lonelier. Then he finds himself in a situation where he needs help, and he understands how it feels when nobody cares. In the end he starts to lend a hand. The film says that empathy is important and that even a small act of help can make a difference.

Two men are shaking hands and one has his arm around the other's shoulder, smiling like a good friend. But behind his back he is holding a knife, ready to stab him. The other man is surprised and has no idea. The cartoon shows a false friend who is two-faced: friendly to your face, but ready to betray you. 'To stab someone in the back' means to betray a person who trusts you. The message is that trust is valuable, and we should be careful who we give it to.

An old companion that has served its family faithfully for years starts to feel unwanted when a new, modern one arrives. It looks outdated next to the new one, and it is afraid of being replaced, so it runs away. But during its journey it shows how loyal and useful it still is, and the family understands they took it for granted. The film says that old does not mean useless: old but gold. We should value the people and things that have always been there for us.

A fat man with a cigar is standing in front of a blackboard like a teacher. On the board he has written: NO + $ = YES. This means that with enough money, any 'no' can become a 'yes'. The artist is criticising corruption and bribery: people in power who can be bought, so rules don't matter if you pay. It suggests that everything has a price. I think corruption destroys trust in society, and that people with integrity, who can't be bought, are very important.

A daughter writes a letter about her father and says he is a liar. Then we see his 'lies': he says he isn't hungry so she can eat, he says he has money when he is out of work, and he says he is fine when he is not. In fact, he is a poor father trying to make ends meet and keep up appearances so his daughter is happy. He sacrifices for his child and hides the truth. His lies are white lies, and they come from unconditional love. The film made me think about everything our parents never tell us.

A man in a suit, with a world map on his back, is standing at one end of a plank on a roof. Another man is standing at the other end and lifting his foot to kick him off. He doesn't understand that the plank only balances because they are both on it: if the 'world' falls, he will fall too. The artist is criticising selfish, short-term thinking in politics. By attacking the world, a leader shoots himself in the foot, because we are all in the same boat. Selfishness backfires.

Every day, a young man helps the people around him. He gives water to a plant, food to a hungry dog and money to a mother and her little daughter in the street. People think he is strange and some look down on him, because he never gets anything back. But he expects nothing in return. What he receives is happiness: the plant grows, the dog follows him and the girl can go to school. He is an unsung hero, and his random acts of kindness show that helping others is a reward itself.

Two women are sitting close together on a sofa, holding hands and talking like best friends. But their shadows on the wall are two snakes ready to bite each other. The cartoon is about fake friends and gossip: people who are sweet to your face but talk behind your back. They are two-faced, and sometimes jealousy is behind it. The message is that we should be careful with friends who gossip about others, because they probably gossip about us too.

The film shows what happens inside Paul's body. His brain wants to play it safe: it is afraid of every risk and keeps him in a dull routine at the office. His heart wants to enjoy life, like going to the beach and eating good food. One day the heart wins and Paul seizes the day. He discovers that taking a risk sometimes makes life wonderful. The film says that we should listen to our gut feeling, let loose sometimes and live life to the fullest, because life is short.

A boxing match: in one corner there is a smartphone with boxing gloves, in the other corner there is a book, and in the middle the referee is a brain. The phone is raising its hands as if it has already won. The cartoon shows that the phone and the book compete for our attention, and the brain decides who wins. The phone usually wins because it is a strong distraction. To give the book a chance, we need willpower and a reading habit, for example reading for 20 minutes before sleep.

A young man has to leave his parents' home: his father thinks it's time for him to leave the nest and stand on his own two feet. The boy sets off, but strange things keep stopping him, and he always comes back home. It's funny, but it also makes us ask what is really holding him back: is he afraid of independence, or homesick before he even leaves? The film shows how hard it is to spread your wings, and that leaving home is a big step for both children and parents.

At the top, a man is running away from another man who holds a knife. But a TV camera shows only a small circle of the scene: the running man's foot looks like he is kicking the other man, who now looks like the victim. The cartoon shows media bias and manipulation: by taking a picture out of context, the media can show the opposite of the truth. A half-truth can be as dangerous as fake news. We should always ask what is outside the frame before we believe something.

An old man runs a small family business, a traditional cheese shop. Times change, big shops take his customers, and it looks like he will go out of business. But he perseveres: he keeps making cheese the slow, traditional way and sticks with it, even when it's hard. In the end people come back for the quality, and he passes down his skills to the next generation, keeping the tradition alive. The film shows that hard work and patience can win, and that some things are worth protecting.

A young girl is walking while looking at her phone, and above her head there is only a small 'like' heart. Behind her, an old man in a wheelchair is reading a book, and above his head there is a huge bookcase full of books. The bookcase is the knowledge in his head. The cartoon shows wisdom that comes with age and reading. The girl is glued to her phone and gets only 'likes'. Young people can learn from their elders, and the generation gap can be closed if we read more.

Pip is a small dog with a big dream: to become a guide dog for visually impaired people. At the guide-dog school she is smaller than the other dogs and fails her tests, so she looks like an underdog. But she doesn't give up. When a real emergency happens, Pip rises to the occasion, uses everything she has learned and saves someone. She proves everyone wrong. The film shows that determination and a big heart are more important than size.

A man and a woman are standing back to back on a broken bridge, with their arms crossed and their heads turned away. Their little child is on a swing hanging from the two broken ends of the bridge. The bridge is the family, and it is falling apart. When parents divorce, the child is caught in the middle, and every move of the parents can make the child fall. The cartoon asks parents to remember that their child depends on both of them, even when they drift apart.

In black-and-white New York, a young man in a dead-end office job meets a woman at a train station when a paper flies from his pile and touches her face. It's love at first sight, but she leaves and it seems like a missed chance. Later he sees her in a window across the street and tries to catch her eye by throwing paper planes. They all miss. But his persistence pays off when the paper planes come to life and bring them together. The film says that if something is meant to be, never give up.

A father and mother are standing behind their little boy. The boy has big white wings, and the father is cutting them off with big scissors while the mother watches. The boy looks sad. The cartoon shows overprotective parents who clip their child's wings: because they are afraid, or because they want to control him, they hold him back and crush his dreams. The child has potential, but he will never fly. Parents should give children freedom to try, make mistakes and grow.

An old lady at a train station buys a packet of cookies and sits next to a young man with headphones. When he takes a cookie from the packet, she is shocked and angry, and they start a silent fight for every cookie. When there is one left, he breaks it in half and gives it to her. She leaves, still angry, and then finds her own packet in her bag: she had been eating his cookies all the time. The film is about jumping to conclusions. Because of prejudice and stereotypes, she misunderstood him. Don't judge a book by its cover.

A family is hugging a father who is coming home with a suitcase, and the children are happy. But the father isn't really coming back: he is walking into a giant smartphone on the wall, and his face is tired. A family photo hangs on the wall. The cartoon shows a parent who is at home but absent, because his mind is in his phone or his work. The family needs quality time, not just his body in the house. We need a better work-life balance and less screen time to be there for our family.

A boy is sent to spend the day with his grandpa, but he is glued to his video game and thinks it will be boring. Grandpa uses his imagination and an old red wagon to turn the day into an amazing adventure: they fly through the sky and fight monsters together. The boy forgets his screen and starts to bond with his grandfather. The film shows the value of quality time with family and reminds us to see the world through a child's eyes. These are the memories that stay with us.

A big crowd of people are standing on an escalator going up. They are all healthy and could easily walk. Next to them, a man on crutches is climbing the stairs alone, with great difficulty. The irony is that the person who needs the escalator most is the only one who can't use it. The cartoon criticises a society that takes things for granted and forgets about accessibility for disabled people. Healthy people take the easy way out, but they should think about others and give their place to those who need it.

We see a man in a suit. His tie has a price tag of $450 and his suit $800, but the top of his head is open and his brain has a tag that says $0. The cartoon criticises people and a society that value looks over brains: they spend a lot of money on clothes and appearance, but nothing on their minds. It is a picture of materialism and wrong priorities. The artist is saying that it is better to invest in yourself, in books and education, because a superficial image is worth nothing without knowledge.
